narrative:
The model estimated a 70% chance that you will leave, which is high enough that the promotion decision treated retention risk as a major concern. In practical terms, it means the model sees your current situation as closer to departure than to staying, so the organization chose not to promote you at this time.

The strongest influence was your total years of experience. Because you have 1–5 years overall, this factor actually pushed the prediction toward staying rather than leaving. The next most influential factor was that you have received other job opportunities while in this role; this pushed strongly toward leaving and was more unusual among employees predicted to stay. Third, your 1–5 years in your current organization also pushed toward leaving. Although your total experience is relatively short, the combination of outside opportunities and your tenure here made the model more concerned about attrition. Other aspects of your profile—such as low pay relative to effort, no bonus, overtime, low support, little recognition, low emotional commitment, psychological exhaustion, and feeling job instability—also contributed to the overall leave prediction, outweighing the stay signal from your total experience.

Before revisiting promotion, the organization should discuss your career path, workload, pay and recognition, training, and the outside opportunities you may be considering. You should clarify what would make you stay and grow here; the organization should separate promotion readiness from attrition risk and address retention concerns directly.
